mcq.QUESTION_DESC: For \( f(x) \) defined on \( (-\pi, \pi) \), the Fourier coefficient \( a_n \) is:
If \( f(x) \) is an even function on \( (-\pi, \pi) \), which Fourier coefficients vanish?
For \( f(x) = x \) defined on \( (-\pi, \pi) \), what type of Fourier series does it have?
The function \( f(x) = x^2 \) on \( (-\pi, \pi) \) has which type of Fourier series?
For \( f(x) \) defined on \( (-\pi, \pi) \), at a point of discontinuity \( x = c \), the Fourier series converges to:

sq.ANSWER:
Upto the stepMarks

\(f(x) = \frac{a_0}{2} + \sum_{n=1}^{\infty} (a_n \cos nx + b_n \sin nx)\)

(2 Mark)

\(\text{where: } a_0 = \frac{1}{\pi} \int_{-\pi}^{\pi} f(x) dx\)

(2 Mark)

\(a_n = \frac{1}{\pi} \int_{-\pi}^{\pi} f(x) \cos nx dx\)

(2 Mark)

\(b_n = \frac{1}{\pi} \int_{-\pi}^{\pi} f(x) \sin nx dx\)

(2 Mark)
sq.QUESTION_DESC: \(\text{Write Fourier series for function in } (-\pi, \pi) \text{ with coefficients formulas.}\)

sq.ANSWER:
Upto the stepMarks

\(\text{For even } f(x), f(-x) = f(x)\)

(2 Mark)

\(\text{Then } b_n = 0 \text{ (sine coefficients vanish)}\)

(2 Mark)

\(a_0 = \frac{2}{\pi} \int_0^{\pi} f(x) dx\)

(2 Mark)

\(a_n = \frac{2}{\pi} \int_0^{\pi} f(x) \cos nx dx\)

(2 Mark)
sq.QUESTION_DESC: \(\text{For even function in } (-\pi, \pi), \text{ what happens to Fourier coefficients?}\)

sq.ANSWER:
Upto the stepMarks

\(\text{Even function: } a_0 = \frac{2}{\pi} \int_0^{\pi} x^2 dx = \frac{2\pi^2}{3}\)

(2 Mark)

\(a_n = \frac{2}{\pi} \int_0^{\pi} x^2 \cos nx dx = \frac{4}{n^2}(-1)^n\)

(2 Mark)

\(\text{Thus } x^2 = \frac{\pi^2}{3} + 4\sum_{n=1}^{\infty} \frac{(-1)^n}{n^2} \cos nx\)

(2 Mark)

\(\text{Put } x = \pi: \pi^2 = \frac{\pi^2}{3} + 4\sum_{n=1}^{\infty} \frac{1}{n^2} \Rightarrow \sum_{n=1}^{\infty} \frac{1}{n^2} = \frac{\pi^2}{6}\)

(2 Mark)
sq.QUESTION_DESC: \(\text{Find Fourier series for } f(x) = x^2 \text{ in } (-\pi, \pi). \text{ Deduce } \sum_{n=1}^{\infty} \frac{1}{n^2}.\)

sq.ANSWER:
Upto the stepMarks

\(\text{For odd } f(x), f(-x) = -f(x)\)

(2 Mark)

\(\text{Then } a_0 = 0, a_n = 0 \text{ (cosine coefficients vanish)}\)

(2 Mark)

\(b_n = \frac{2}{\pi} \int_0^{\pi} f(x) \sin nx dx\)

(2 Mark)

\(\text{Series becomes sine series: } f(x) = \sum_{n=1}^{\infty} b_n \sin nx\)

(2 Mark)
sq.QUESTION_DESC: \(\text{For odd function in } (-\pi, \pi), \text{ what happens to Fourier coefficients?}\)

lq.ANSWER:
StepMarks
Since \(f(x)\) is odd, \(a_0=0\), \(a_n=0\)(2)
\(b_n=\frac{2}{\pi}\int_0^{\pi}x\cos x\sin nx\,dx=\frac{1}{\pi}\int_0^{\pi}x[\sin(n+1)x+\sin(n-1)x]dx\)(3)
For \(n=1\): \(b_1=\frac{2}{\pi}\int_0^{\pi}x\cos x\sin x\,dx=\frac{1}{\pi}\int_0^{\pi}x\sin 2x\,dx=-\frac{1}{2}\)(3)
For \(n\neq1\): \(b_n=(-1)^n\frac{2n}{n^2-1}\)(4)
Thus, \(x\cos x=-\frac{1}{2}\sin x+2\sum_{n=2}^{\infty}(-1)^n\frac{n}{n^2-1}\sin nx\)(3)
